passage: Counsellor's note, Tuesday. I am Sharmila, hostel counsellor. Last night a student, Minakshi, told me she heard a loud scream from the lane behind the hostel around ten. She froze at the window, unsure whether it was friends playing, a film on someone's phone or trouble. She wanted to run down. I said that rushing in alone would not be wise. Instead she called the warden, who sent the security guard. It turned out a stray dog had bitten someone's bag and a girl had shrieked in fright. Nobody was hurt. Minakshi said her heart raced for an hour. I praised her for calling and not going alone, and I will check on her this week.

qa.q: Who did Minakshi call?
qa.a: Minakshi called the warden.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling at the window, and what does the racing heart suggest?
qa.a: Minakshi was frightened and unsure whether it was play or danger, and wanted to rush out. The racing heart suggests she took the scream seriously and it stayed with her.

qa.q: What was the safer choice than running into the lane?
qa.a: Calling the warden so the security guard could go was safer than rushing in alone.

qa.q: How might the girl who shrieked have felt afterwards?
qa.a: She had been frightened by the dog, so she may have felt startled and shaken, and possibly embarrassed that it caused alarm.

grounding: Counsellor's note on a young adult hearing a scream and choosing to call the warden and guard instead of ignoring it or rushing in alone.

passage:
Sat. 11:15 pm. Heard a scream from the street below the flat. Maria and I froze mid-chat. My first thought was a horror film someone was streaming. Then it came again, higher, and a voice shouting "Leave me alone!" My legs wanted to run downstairs. Maria held my arm and said, "Do not go alone." We called the emergency number and told them the address and what we heard. Then we watched from the window. Two neighbours came out and a police vehicle arrived. It was a quarrel that got out of hand. Nobody was badly hurt. I am still shaky, but I am glad we called.
- Simran

qa.q: What did Simran and Maria do after the second scream?
qa.a: They called the emergency number and gave the address and what they heard.

qa.q: What did Simran feel when the scream came again, and how do you know?
qa.a: Simran felt alarmed and wanted to run downstairs, and the first guess of a film gave way to worry once the words "Leave me alone!" were heard.

qa.q: Which choice was wise, and why?
qa.a: Calling the emergency number instead of going down alone was wise, because trained people could reach the street safely.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Simran wanted to run down?
qa.a: Maria was probably worried about Simran's safety, which is why Maria held the arm and said not to go alone.

grounding: Diary entry about hearing a scream, weighing play, film or danger, and calling emergency help instead of ignoring or rushing in alone.

passage: At the town fair in Beawar, the giant wheel had been full of shrieks all evening, the happy kind that rise and fall with each turn. Wasim and Kashish were buying roasted chana when one scream didn't fall. It went on, high and thin, from the top car, and the wheel had stopped. Kashish grabbed Wasim's sleeve. "That's not fun screaming." Wasim squinted. A boy was half standing in the swaying car, and a woman was pulling at him. Wasim's feet were already moving toward the wheel's frame; he had climbed trees all his childhood. Kashish held on. "No. Police booth. Now." They ran the thirty steps to the tent with the loudspeaker, and Wasim told the constable exactly where. The constable radioed the operator, the announcer told everyone to stay seated, and two fair staff with a harness went up the service ladder. The boy was down in ten minutes, crying but unhurt.

qa.q: What were Wasim and Kashish buying?
qa.a: Roasted chana.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel when this scream didn't fall, and why?
qa.a: Kashish felt a jolt of alarm because the scream didn't rise and fall like the fun shrieks; it went on, high and thin, and the wheel had stopped.

qa.q: Why was going to the police booth wiser than climbing the frame?
qa.a: The constable could get the operator to act, the announcer to keep everyone seated and trained staff to climb with a harness, while climbing alone could have put another person in danger.

qa.q: What might the woman in the top car have been feeling?
qa.a: She was likely terrified, struggling to keep the boy seated in a swaying car, and relieved when help came up the ladder.

grounding: Shows young adults telling a playful scream from a dangerous one and alerting the police rather than rushing in alone.

passage: At two in the morning, a scream came through the thin wall of Hiroshi's flat in Osaka, then a thud. He sat up. His neighbour, Selin, sometimes played online games late and yelled at them. But this sounded different: a word, cut off, then silence. Hiroshi's first thought was to pound on her door himself. His second was that he had no idea who else was in there. He rang the building's night manager, Mr. Sato, and then the police emergency number, giving the flat number and describing the sounds. Mr. Sato came up within minutes, and when two officers arrived, he knocked and called Selin's name. A pale Selin opened the door, holding a towel to her forehead. She had slipped in the shower and hit her head. The officers called an ambulance, and Mr. Sato stayed with her until it came.

qa.q: Who was the building's night manager?
qa.a: Mr. Sato.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he heard the scream?
qa.a: Hiroshi felt alarmed but uncertain, wondering if it was Selin yelling at a game or real danger, and was wary because he didn't know who else was inside.

qa.q: Why was calling the manager and police a good choice?
qa.a: It brought help without Hiroshi rushing into an unknown situation alone, and it meant Selin got an ambulance quickly after her fall.

qa.q: How might Selin have felt when the door was knocked on?
qa.a: Selin was probably shaken and in pain, and relieved that someone had heard and come to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing whether a scream is play or danger and calling the building manager and police rather than ignoring it or going in alone.

passage:
Just after midnight in the women's hostel, a scream cut through the corridor, then stopped.
Vidya sat up in bed. "Did you hear that?"
Mehak didn't take out her earphones. "Room 14. They watch horror films every Friday."
It was Friday. But the scream had come from the direction of the stairwell, not Room 14, and a thud had followed it.
Vidya's heart was pounding. Going alone into a dark stairwell felt foolish. Pretending she hadn't heard felt worse. She picked up her phone and called the security desk. "There was a scream and a thud near the east stairwell, second floor. Could someone check?"
Within three minutes the night guard came up with a torch, the warden behind her. They found a first-year sitting on the landing, clutching her ankle after missing a step in the dark. The warden called the hostel doctor and stayed with her.

qa.q: On which night did Room 14 usually watch horror films?
qa.a: They watch horror films every Friday.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she weighed what to do?
qa.a: Vidya felt scared and uneasy, heart pounding, unsure whether it was a film or real danger, and unwilling either to ignore it or go alone.

qa.q: Which choice did Vidya make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She called the security desk with the exact place, so trained people could check quickly without her walking into danger alone.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have reacted differently from Vidya?
qa.a: Mehak had her earphones in and linked the scream to Room 14's Friday films, so she didn't notice the thud or the direction it came from.

grounding: On hearing a scream, a young adult weighs whether it is play, a film or danger, and calls security instead of ignoring it or rushing in alone.
